# MIOREK LAB // CLINICAL SPEC ARCHIVE

> Independent, never-sponsored head-to-head spec comparisons. Each entry: 4-spec matrix with winner, one fatal flaw per product, and a buy-if verdict.

## Oura Ring 4 vs Samsung Galaxy Ring (WEARABLE TECH) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#01_smart_rings
- Prices (USD list): Oura Ring 4 $349; Samsung Galaxy Ring $399
- Subscription Fee: Oura Ring 4 = $5.99/mo or $69.99/yr; Samsung Galaxy Ring = No Subscription; winner: Samsung Galaxy Ring. Over 3 years Oura costs $349 + $209.97 membership = $558.97; Galaxy Ring has no recurring fee.
- Phone Compatibility: Oura Ring 4 = iOS & Android; Samsung Galaxy Ring = Android Only (Samsung Health); winner: Oura Ring 4. Galaxy Ring needs an Android phone that runs Samsung Health; it does not work with iPhone.
- Battery Life: Oura Ring 4 = 5-8 Days (Varies by Size); Samsung Galaxy Ring = Up to 6-7 Days (Varies by Size); winner: Oura Ring 4. Oura rates the Ring 4 at 5-8 days; Samsung rates sizes 5-11 at up to 6 days and sizes 12-13 at up to 7.
- Charger: Oura Ring 4 = Size-Specific Charging Dock; Samsung Galaxy Ring = Charging Case (361mAh Battery); winner: Samsung Galaxy Ring. Galaxy Ring's case carries its own battery for charging on the go; Oura Ring 4 ships with a dock.
- Fatal flaw, Oura Ring 4: Without the $5.99/mo membership the app shows only three daily scores (Sleep, Readiness, Activity); the newer Oura Ring 5 is $399.
- Fatal flaw, Samsung Galaxy Ring: No iPhone support at all, and Samsung's US store currently lists some sizes as out of stock.
- Buy Oura Ring 4 if: You use an iPhone, or want 5-8 day battery life and don't mind paying $69.99 a year.
- Buy Samsung Galaxy Ring if: You use Android and want no subscription plus a charging case with its own battery.

## Sony WF-1000XM5 vs Technics EAH-AZ80 (AUDIOPHILE / BINAURAL TEST) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#02_flagship_tws
- Prices (USD list): Sony WF-1000XM5 $299; Technics EAH-AZ80 $299
- Active Noise Cancelling: Sony WF-1000XM5 = Industry #1 (Foam Tips); Technics EAH-AZ80 = Top-Tier (Silicone Tips); winner: Sony WF-1000XM5. Sony deletes low-end subway and cabin rumble more aggressively.
- Binaural L/R Separation: Sony WF-1000XM5 = Warm, Center-Focused; Technics EAH-AZ80 = 10mm Free-Edge Wide Stage; winner: Technics EAH-AZ80. Technics reveals pinpoint Left/Right instrument layering without mud.
- Multipoint Connection: Sony WF-1000XM5 = 2 Devices Max; Technics EAH-AZ80 = 3 Devices Simultaneously; winner: Technics EAH-AZ80. AZ80 switches between PC, Phone, and Tablet seamlessly.
- Ear Tip Comfort & Durability: Sony WF-1000XM5 = Polyurethane (Degrades in 6mo); Technics EAH-AZ80 = 7 Sizes Medical Silicone; winner: Technics EAH-AZ80. Sony's stock foam tips trap sweat and crumble over time.
- Fatal flaw, Sony WF-1000XM5: Glossy slippery shell is easy to drop; stock foam tips wear out fast.
- Fatal flaw, Technics EAH-AZ80: Slightly larger charging case and less aggressive high-frequency ANC than Sony.
- Buy Sony WF-1000XM5 if: You prioritize maximum noise isolation on flights and heavy bass punch.
- Buy Technics EAH-AZ80 if: You want audiophile Left/Right separation, 3-way multipoint, and all-day comfort.

## Anker Prime 200W vs UGREEN Nexode 130W (DESK & EDC POWER) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#03_power_banks
- Prices (USD list): Anker Prime 200W $139; UGREEN Nexode 130W $89
- Total Dual-Port Output: Anker Prime 200W = 200W Max (100W + 100W); UGREEN Nexode 130W = 130W Max (100W + 30W); winner: Anker Prime 200W. Anker charges two laptops at 100W each at the same time.
- Recharging Input Speed: Anker Prime 200W = 100W USB-C (or Pogo Base); UGREEN Nexode 130W = 65W USB-C Input; winner: Anker Prime 200W. Anker refills in ~75 mins at 100W (USB-C or base); UGREEN takes about 2 hours at 65W.
- Price-to-Performance: Anker Prime 200W = $139 ($0.70 / Watt); UGREEN Nexode 130W = $89 (Often on Sale); winner: UGREEN Nexode 130W. Single-laptop users save $50 with UGREEN while keeping 100W single-port speed.
- Smart Display & App: Anker Prime 200W = Smart Display + Bluetooth App; UGREEN Nexode 130W = Smart Display Only (No App); winner: Anker Prime 200W. Anker's Bluetooth app shows detailed charging stats; UGREEN shows live wattage on its screen only.
- Fatal flaw, Anker Prime 200W: Expensive; pogo-pin charging base is sold separately.
- Fatal flaw, UGREEN Nexode 130W: Drops second USB-C port to 30W when main port pulls 100W.
- Buy Anker Prime 200W if: You carry two high-draw devices (MacBook + gaming handheld) and want 100W fast recharge.
- Buy UGREEN Nexode 130W if: You only need to charge ONE laptop + a phone and want the best value under $90.

## Sony WH-1000XM5 vs Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen) (AUDIOPHILE / BINAURAL TEST) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#04_anc_headphones
- Prices (USD list): Sony WH-1000XM5 $399; Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen) $449
- Foldability & Build: Sony WH-1000XM5 = Does NOT Fold (Weak Hinge); Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen) = Folds Flat & Compact; winner: Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen). Sony's non-folding hinge is a common failure point when stuffed in backpacks.
- Microphone Call Quality: Sony WH-1000XM5 = 4 Beamforming Mics + AI Noise Reduction; Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen) = Good Indoors, Weaker in Noise; winner: Sony WH-1000XM5. Sony's AI voice pickup isolates your voice better in loud cafes and streets.
- Spatial / Binaural Stage: Sony WH-1000XM5 = Narrower, Bass-Forward; Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen) = Bose Immersive Audio (Wide); winner: Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen). Bose creates a wider out-of-head 3D soundstage for binaural tracks.
- List Price: Sony WH-1000XM5 = $399 (Sony MSRP); Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen) = $449 (Bose MSRP); winner: Sony WH-1000XM5. Same 30-hour ANC battery rating, but Sony costs $50 less at list.
- Fatal flaw, Sony WH-1000XM5: Bulky carrying case because it doesn't fold; shallow earcups touch larger ears.
- Fatal flaw, Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen): $50 more expensive, and Immersive Audio cuts battery to as little as 18 hours.
- Buy Sony WH-1000XM5 if: You take frequent work calls and want flagship ANC for $50 less.
- Buy Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen) if: You value a folding design, plush comfort, and wide spatial audio.

## BenQ ScreenBar Pro vs Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+ (DESK & EDC POWER) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#05_monitor_lights
- Prices (USD list): BenQ ScreenBar Pro $139; Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+ $69
- Auto-Presence Sensor: BenQ ScreenBar Pro = Presence Sensor (Auto On/Off); Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+ = No Presence Sensor (Remote Control); winner: BenQ ScreenBar Pro. BenQ turns on automatically when you sit down and off when you leave.
- Published Brightness: BenQ ScreenBar Pro = 1000 Lux Center, 85x50cm Coverage; Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+ = 700-1200 Lux (Varies by Listing); winner: BenQ ScreenBar Pro. BenQ rates 1000 lux at center over an 85x50cm area; Quntis brightness claims vary by listing.
- Controls: BenQ ScreenBar Pro = On-Bar Controls (No Remote); Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+ = Wireless Remote Controller; winner: Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+. Quntis puts dimming on a wireless remote you keep on the desk; ScreenBar Pro is adjusted on the bar itself.
- Price-to-Value Ratio: BenQ ScreenBar Pro = $139; Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+ = $69 (Remote Included); winner: Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+. Quntis costs about half as much and still includes a wireless remote.
- Fatal flaw, BenQ ScreenBar Pro: Costs twice as much as the Quntis; no wireless remote dial on the Pro model.
- Fatal flaw, Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+: No presence sensor, and its brightness figures vary between listings.
- Buy BenQ ScreenBar Pro if: You want automatic on/off presence sensing and officially rated 1000-lux center brightness.
- Buy Quntis ScreenLinear Pro+ if: You want a remote-controlled monitor light for about half the price.

## Logitech MX Master 3S vs Keychron M6 (1000Hz) (DESK SETUP / MICE) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#06_productivity_mice
- Prices (USD list): Logitech MX Master 3S $99; Keychron M6 (1000Hz) $49
- Polling Rate & Sensor: Logitech MX Master 3S = 125Hz (Measured, Not Published); Keychron M6 (1000Hz) = 1000Hz PixArt 3395; winner: Keychron M6 (1000Hz). At 125Hz the MX reports position 8x less often than the Keychron's 1000Hz.
- Weight: Logitech MX Master 3S = 141g; Keychron M6 (1000Hz) = 78-86g (Varies by Version); winner: Keychron M6 (1000Hz). Keychron is at least 55g lighter, depending on the version you buy.
- Scroll Wheel: Logitech MX Master 3S = MagSpeed Electromagnetic; Keychron M6 (1000Hz) = Infinite Scroll + Side Wheel; winner: Logitech MX Master 3S. Logitech rates MagSpeed at 1,000 lines per second and precise enough to stop on a pixel.
- List Price: Logitech MX Master 3S = $99 (Logitech MSRP); Keychron M6 (1000Hz) = $49 (Keychron List); winner: Keychron M6 (1000Hz). Keychron costs $50 less and still has a side wheel and a 3395 sensor.
- Fatal flaw, Logitech MX Master 3S: 141g and a 125Hz report rate; heavy and slow-reporting next to gaming-grade mice.
- Fatal flaw, Keychron M6 (1000Hz): Weight, polling and sensor differ by version, so check the exact SKU before buying.
- Buy Logitech MX Master 3S if: You want MagSpeed electromagnetic scrolling and Easy-Switch across three devices.
- Buy Keychron M6 (1000Hz) if: You use a 120Hz+ monitor and want a lighter 1000Hz mouse for half the price.

## Wooting 60HE+ vs Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini (DESK SETUP / KEYBOARDS) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#07_hall_effect_keyboards
- Prices (USD list): Wooting 60HE+ $154; Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini $179
- Software: Wooting 60HE+ = Wootility (Runs in Browser); Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini = Razer Synapse (Desktop App); winner: Wooting 60HE+. Wootility configures the board from a web browser; Razer's full settings need the Synapse app.
- Case Material: Wooting 60HE+ = ABS Plastic Case (605g); Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini = 5052 Aluminum Top Case; winner: Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini. Razer uses a brushed 5052 aluminum top case; the 60HE+ case is ABS plastic.
- Availability: Wooting 60HE+ = Sold Out on Wooting US Store; Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini = Stocked at Major Retailers; winner: Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini. Wooting's US store lists the 60HE+ as sold out; its successor, the 60HE v2, lists at $239.99.
- List Price: Wooting 60HE+ = $154 (Wooting Store); Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini = $179 (Razer MSRP); winner: Wooting 60HE+. Wooting is $25 cheaper at list price, when it's in stock.
- Fatal flaw, Wooting 60HE+: Sold out on Wooting's US store with an ABS plastic case; the successor 60HE v2 lists at $239.99.
- Fatal flaw, Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini: Costs $25 more, and full profile control needs the Razer Synapse desktop app.
- Buy Wooting 60HE+ if: You want the lower list price and browser-based Wootility setup, and can wait for stock.
- Buy Razer Huntsman V3 Pro Mini if: You want an aluminum top case and a keyboard you can buy at retailers today.

## Fanttik E1 MAX Electric vs HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual) (DESK SETUP / REPAIR TOOLS) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#08_precision_screwdrivers
- Prices (USD list): Fanttik E1 MAX Electric $79; HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual) $19
- Drive Mechanism: Fanttik E1 MAX Electric = Electric 200 RPM (0.05 / 0.2 N·m); HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual) = Manual Only (No Battery); winner: Fanttik E1 MAX Electric. The E1 MAX spins screws out at 200 RPM in two torque gears; the HOTO pen is turned by hand.
- Bit Count: Fanttik E1 MAX Electric = 50 S2 Magnetic Bits; HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual) = 24 S2 Steel Bits; winner: Fanttik E1 MAX Electric. Fanttik includes 50 S2 bits; HOTO includes 24 S2-steel bits.
- Bit Storage: Fanttik E1 MAX Electric = Separate Aluminum Magnetic Case; HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual) = Stored Inside the Pen Body; winner: HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual). HOTO keeps its bits in a magnetic compartment inside the pen; Fanttik's bits live in a separate case.
- List Price: Fanttik E1 MAX Electric = $79 (Fanttik List); HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual) = $19 (HOTO Store); winner: HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual). HOTO is $60 cheaper at list price; Fanttik's own store currently has the E1 MAX on sale for $39.99.
- Fatal flaw, Fanttik E1 MAX Electric: Needs its 350mAh battery charged, motor torque tops out at 0.2 N·m, and the bits ride in a separate case.
- Fatal flaw, HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual): Manual only: no motor and no LED light, with 24 bits instead of 50.
- Buy Fanttik E1 MAX Electric if: You repair electronics often and want 50 bits, a 200 RPM motor and built-in LED lights.
- Buy HOTO Screwdriver Pen (Manual) if: You want a $19 aluminum pen that keeps its 24 bits inside and never needs charging.

## Moondrop CHU II vs 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2 (AUDIO / WIRED IEMS) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#09_budget_iems
- Prices (USD list): Moondrop CHU II $18; 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2 $24
- Impedance: Moondrop CHU II = 18Ω; 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2 = 32Ω; winner: Moondrop CHU II. Lower impedance is easier to drive from a phone or a small USB-C dongle.
- Sensitivity: Moondrop CHU II = 119dB/Vrms; 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2 = 108dB/V; winner: Moondrop CHU II. Moondrop's rating is 11 dB higher per volt, so CHU II plays louder at the same volume setting.
- Rated Low-End Limit: Moondrop CHU II = 15Hz (15Hz-38kHz); 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2 = 10Hz (10Hz-20kHz); winner: 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2. Zero:2 is rated down to 10Hz; CHU II is rated from 15Hz but extends higher, to 38kHz.
- List Price: Moondrop CHU II = $18 (Launch MSRP); 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2 = $24 (Linsoul); winner: Moondrop CHU II. CHU II launched at $18.99 and now sells for about $22.99 at Linsoul; Zero:2 lists at $24.99.
- Fatal flaw, Moondrop CHU II: Moondrop lists only the IEMs, one 3.5mm cable and a storage bag in the box (no mic listed), and retail has crept up to about $22.99.
- Fatal flaw, 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2: Rated 32Ω / 108dB/V, so it needs more volume than CHU II, and Linsoul's standard listing is 3.5mm with no mic.
- Buy Moondrop CHU II if: You want the easiest-to-drive, lowest-priced wired IEM for a phone or USB-C dongle.
- Buy 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2 if: You want Crinacle's Zero:2 tuning with a rated 10Hz low end and can spend about $6 more.

## Anker Prime Charger 100W vs UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port (TRAVEL / CHARGERS) — https://miorek7.github.io/miorek-lab/#10_travel_chargers
- Prices (USD list): Anker Prime Charger 100W $69; UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port $54
- Ports: Anker Prime Charger 100W = 2× USB-C + 1× USB-A; UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port = 3× USB-C + 1× USB-A; winner: UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port. UGREEN adds a fourth port; both deliver up to 100W from a single USB-C port.
- Weight: Anker Prime Charger 100W = 170g (6 oz); UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port = 210g (7.4 oz); winner: Anker Prime Charger 100W. Anker is 40g lighter in a travel bag.
- Body Size: Anker Prime Charger 100W = 43.5 × 29 × 67.8 mm; UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port = 70.8 × 42.9 × 32.7 mm; winner: Anker Prime Charger 100W. About 85.5 cm³ for Anker vs 99.3 cm³ for UGREEN (prongs excluded).
- List Price: Anker Prime Charger 100W = $69 (Anker List); UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port = $54 (UGREEN Store); winner: UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port. UGREEN lists at $54.99 vs $69.99; Anker's own store has a Black Friday price of $45.99 through Nov 30.
- Fatal flaw, Anker Prime Charger 100W: Only three ports, total output drops to 89W with all three in use, and it lists $15 higher.
- Fatal flaw, UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port: 40g heavier and bulkier, and UGREEN's US product page does not spell out its multi-port power split.
- Buy Anker Prime Charger 100W if: You want the smallest, lightest 100W charger (170g) for a laptop bag.
- Buy UGREEN Nexode 100W 4-Port if: You charge four devices at once and want the lower $54.99 list price.
